tables.one_row: one citation or order, full 64-column file
tables.connects: one row per distinct EVENT_NO with its INSPECTION_BEGIN_DT and INSPECTION_END_DT; MINE_ID, quotes stripped, matches MINE_ID on LABOR__FED_MSHA_ACCIDENTS

columns.name: EVENT_NO
columns.plain: the id of the inspection visit that produced the citation
columns.watch: Citing inspections only. Inspections that found nothing are not here either.

columns.name: INSPECTION_BEGIN_DT
columns.plain: the day that inspection visit started
columns.watch: Fill not measured; two columns found by name here were empty. Strip quotes before casting; an empty value is a pair of quotes, not NULL.

columns.name: INSPECTION_END_DT
columns.plain: the day that inspection visit ended
columns.watch: Fill not measured. Strip quotes before casting; an empty value is a pair of quotes, not NULL.

columns.name: MINE_ID
columns.plain: the mine safety agency's id for the cited mine, wrapped in quote marks here
columns.watch: Every landing value is wrapped in literal double quotes. Strip before joining. This copy holds 3,087,266 rows against the mart's 3,087,265.

columns.name: VIOLATION_ISSUE_DT
columns.plain: the day the inspector wrote the citation

columns.name: COAL_METAL_IND
columns.plain: C for a coal mine, M for metal or non-metal

tables.connects: MINE_ID matches MINE_ID on LABOR__FED_MSHA_VIOLATIONS

columns.name: ACCIDENT_DATE
columns.plain: the calendar day the accident happened at the mine
columns.watch: Starts in 2000. Surface mines shut for winter in many states, so a winter dip can be activity.

columns.name: MINE_ID
columns.plain: the mine safety agency's id for one mine
columns.watch: 13,708 mines have an accident row against 32,133 with a citation row. The gap test runs on the 13,338 shared mines.

columns.name: DEGREE_INJURY
columns.plain: how bad it was, in words: days away from work, restricted duty, accident only, and so on

columns.name: IS_FATALITY
columns.plain: true when someone died; 1,208 rows are true

columns.name: NO_INJURIES
columns.plain: how many people were hurt in that one event, usually 1

columns.name: COAL_METAL_IND
columns.plain: C for a coal mine, M for metal or non-metal

idea: Do work sites in the same industry and the same state all report injury rates that run high or low together, beyond what their size explains?
why: If whole industry-and-state pockets sit far from the national rate, something local is moving everyone, like state rules, one dominant employer or how people report. If not, injury rates are just an industry fact.

columns.name: NAICS_CODE
columns.plain: the six-digit industry code the site picked for itself
columns.watch: Fill not measured. Code editions are mixed; map to one edition or use the first 4 digits.

columns.name: NAICS_YEAR
columns.plain: which edition of the industry code list the site used, such as 2012, 2017 or 2022
columns.watch: Runs from 0 to 180175 in the 2025 table. Mixed and partly junk.

columns.name: STATE
columns.plain: the two-letter state the work site is in
columns.watch: Fill not measured. No flag for state-run OSHA programs, so a state effect cannot be split from a reporting-rule effect.

columns.name: SIZE
columns.plain: the employer size band as a code; coded value, look at distinct values first

columns.name: ANNUAL_AVERAGE_EMPLOYEES
columns.plain: average number of workers at the site over the year

columns.name: TOTAL_HOURS_WORKED
columns.plain: hours all workers put in that year, the bottom of any injury rate
columns.watch: 1,065B hours against 138.8M employees, about 7,672 per employee. Keep rows between 800 and 3,000 hours per employee, 88% of rows.

columns.name: TOTAL_INJURIES
columns.plain: count of work injuries the site wrote on the form that year
columns.watch: Multi-site filers report zero injuries 49 to 79% of the time against 6.7% for ordinary rows. One big public filer makes a state look safe.

columns.name: TOTAL_DAFW_CASES
columns.plain: count of cases where the worker missed days of work

columns.name: TOTAL_DJTR_CASES
columns.plain: count of cases where the worker was moved or put on light duty

columns.name: ESTABLISHMENT_ID
columns.plain: OSHA's id for one work site, the same number year to year

columns.name: YEAR_FILING_FOR
columns.plain: the calendar year the form covers; one value per table

idea: Which employers got caught working kids illegally and still collect federal contract money afterward?
why: It would be a named list of companies the government fined with one hand and paid with the other. No matches can just mean the contract sits with a parent company at another address.

tables.one_row: one closed wage-and-hour case against one employer

idea: Which employers flagged as repeat wage cheats keep getting new federal contract money year after year?
why: It would show the government keeps paying companies it has already caught shorting workers more than once. A miss means repeat violators are mostly small local shops, or the name match cannot see the real contracting company.
